items.title: Ship propellers "freeze" under water sometimes
items.body:

<!-- Make sure the bug still occurs after you have uninstalled all mods. -->
<!-- Make sure your bug hasn't been reported by someone else already. -->
<!-- If you are sure you found a new bug, please fill out all fields below as best as you can. -->

**What happened?**
I'm using some of my boats and ships that have worked fine before, but now the propeller sometimes freezes up and won't rotate under water. 
If I spawn it in the air it rotates just fine, as soon as the ship hits the water it freezes up and neither the propeller nor the boat move. Same if i spawn it in the water, the prop won't move.
It doesn't happen on all my ships/boats, just on some like the two linked below.

**How can we reproduce this bug?**
Spawn in either of these ship or boat in the air and the props spin properly, spawn it in the water or let it fall into the water and the props seize up for some reason.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3498159178

items.title: Video support: video_url content parts are silently dropped
items.body:
## Summary

A `video_url` content part is **silently dropped**. The model answers from the surrounding text as though no video was sent — a plausible answer with no signal that the video never arrived. This issue scopes what it takes to serve video properly, and what to ship first.

Found while building the `vision-fidelity` gate (#513). Everything below is verified against the tree and the shipped checkpoints rather than inferred from the HF implementation.

## Today's behaviour

Two drop sites, both silent:

- `crates/spark-server/src/openai/chat_message.rs:326` — Chat Completions: `_ => {} // ignore unknown part types`
- `crates/spark-server/src/openai/chat_message.rs:255` — Responses API: the `input_image | image_url | image` arm simply does not match, and there is no `else`

`ContentPart` (`crates/spark-server/src/ir/message.rs:143`) has `Text` and `Image` only, with a doc comment already anticipating this: *"Open for future modalities (audio, video, file)."*

## What is already in place

More than expected — the model side is not starting from zero.

- **`temporal_patch_size = 2` is real and honoured.** `vision_preprocess.rs:185` builds patches with a `T` axis and fills it by **duplicating the still image** `tp` times (`:193`). A video frame-pair is the case that axis was designed for.
- **MRoPE has three independent position streams.** `ops::rope_mrope_interleaved` (`layers/ops/embeddings.rs:160`) takes `pos_t`, `pos_h`, `pos_w` as separate device pointers and assigns rotary pairs round-robin by `pair_idx % 3`. The kernel needs nothing new.
- **`<|video_pad|>` exists in the tokenizer** and the bundled chat template already branches on `videos` / `video_count` / `video_pad`.
- **The checkpoints declare a full video processor.** `unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-NVFP4` → `processor_config.json.video_processor`; `unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` → a dedicated `video_preprocessor_config.json`:

  ```
  do_sample_frames: true,  fps: 2,  min_frames: 4,  max_frames: 768,
  merge_size: 2,  temporal_patch_size: 2,  size.longest_edge: 25165824
  ```

  Note that bound is **larger than the image bound** (25165824 vs 16777216) and lives in the same file. The image-bound reader deliberately addresses `image_processor` explicitly so it cannot pick this up; a video path must read the video one just as deliberately.

## What is missing

### 1. The position builder is image-shaped

`model/trait_impl/prefill_b/upload_meta.rs:111-165` is where this actually bites. It walks `vision_image_grids` as `(gh, gw)` pairs and, for each pad run, emits `T = base` **constant across the whole item**, advancing `current_pos += max(gh, gw)` afterwards.

That is correct for a still. For video, `T` must advance **per frame**, so the item's grid needs a temporal extent: `(t, gh, gw)`, with `t = frames / temporal_patch_size`. This is the single most invasive change, because the grid vector is threaded through the co-dispatch path (`vision_grid_base`, `vision_owned_images`) and shared across concurrently-batched requests.

### 2. Frame decode

The hard dependency question. `spark-model` currently pulls `image = { features = ["jpeg", "png"] }` and nothing else. Options, roughly in order of cost:

- **Animated GIF / APNG** — pure Rust, `image` crate feature flag only, no system dependency. Enough to prove the whole pipeline end to end.
- **MP4/H.264** — what users will actually send. Needs a real decoder (`openh264-sys2` vendored + `cc`, or ffmpeg bindings with a system dependency). This is the decision that sets the schedule.

Frame **sampling** is a separate concern from decode and is specified by the checkpoint: `fps: 2`, clamped to `[min_frames, max_frames]`.

### 3. Token accounting and splicing

`<|video_pad|>` runs instead of `<|image_pad|>`, with `t * gh * gw / merge²` merged tokens per video. Every place that counts image pads (`image_count()`, `image_pad_counts`, the Jinja marker expansion) needs the video equivalent.

### 4. Memory

ViT attention is O(patches²) and already clamps: the encoder caps at `CEILING_MAX_PATCHES = 16384` and logs when a checkpoint asks for more. A video is `t` frames of a full patch grid, so it hits that ceiling far sooner than a still. Frame count, resolution and the ceiling have to be reasoned about together, not independently.

## Proposed order

1. **Reject explicitly** (small, standalone, ship first). Turn both silent drops into a 400 naming the reason, matching the existing remote-URL rejection in `api/chat/msg_entry.rs:75-84`. A wrong answer becomes an honest error, which is strictly better than today and worth having regardless of when the rest lands.
2. **`ContentPart::Video` + wire parsing** on both APIs, base64 `data:` only.
3. **Decode + sampling**, GIF/APNG first to prove the pipeline, container format decided separately.
4. **`(t, gh, gw)` grids** through the preprocessor, the encoder, and `upload_meta`'s MRoPE builder — the real work.
5. **Video-token splicing** and the `<|video_pad|>` accounting.
6. **A short-video leg in the `vision-fidelity` gate**, with a tiny committed fixture provisioned the same way the eight image fixtures are, a deterministic geometry assertion (frame count × grid is arithmetic, exactly like the image rungs), and a no-video control so the leg cannot pass vacuously.

Steps 1 and 2 are independently useful. Step 4 is the one that touches the hot prefill path and deserves its own review.

## Related

- #513 — the vision gate and the resolution-bound work this came out of
- Remote image URLs are rejected today by design; an operator opt-in to fetch them is tracked separately

items.title: OF-054 — Plan ML model readiness and first model strategy

milestone.title: M4 — Camera-Based ML Readiness
milestone.description: Decide when ML starts, data rules, model strategy, OpenRiverCam comparison

items.body:
## Objective

Create a clear plan for when and how OpenFloodAI should start ML model work, while keeping the project camera-first.

In simple terms: before we train or plug in a model, we need to decide what data, labels, safety rules, and success checks are required. The first ML direction should support camera-based flood evidence, not replace the project with a general weather or flood-forecasting system.

## Background

The project is not ready for full ML model implementation yet. We first need better validation evidence, better frame sampling, and a small labelled dataset that we trust.

This issue is for planning only. It should not train a model yet.

We also received useful engineering input that OpenRiverCam is a strong open-source reference for camera-based water level, velocity, and discharge. Google Flood Forecasting / OpenHydroNet is useful for future basin-level forecasting research, but it is not the immediate camera MVP.

## Camera-First Boundary

Document this clearly:

```text
OpenFloodAI should focus first on a camera-based approach.

The core product is local camera evidence, human labels, machine comparison, and review.

Weather, rainfall, earthquake, hydrology, and forecasting data are useful future cross-checks, but they should not become the main MVP scope.
```

Plain-language version:

```text
First make the camera workflow reliable.
Later use rainfall, earthquake, and forecast data to double-check risk.
```

## Dependencies

This planning can start now, but final ML implementation should wait until at least these are clearer:

- #104: machine evidence samples frames across the labelled window
- #81: validation scorecard exists
- #106: review evidence images are meaningful
- #111: labelled data quality checklist exists

## Required Discussion Areas

Document a simple ML readiness plan covering:

- what labels we need first
- how many example videos or labelled windows we should collect before trying ML
- what counts as good training data
- what should stay local/private
- how OpenRiverCam may fit as upstream camera-monitoring inspiration or integration
- how Google Flood Forecasting may fit later as forecasting research, not immediate MVP implementation
- whether open-source segmentation models can help with assisted labelling
- whether Google ML, Vertex AI, or AutoML could help later
- what a first camera-based model should predict
- what metrics we should use to decide if the model is improving
- what safety boundaries must remain in place

## Tool And Model Comparison To Include

Include or link to a comparison table like this:

| Option | Best For | Not Best For | Recommended Use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenRiverCam / pyOpenRiverCam | Camera-based river water level, velocity, and discharge | General flood forecasting for an entire basin | Strong inspiration and possible future integration for upstream camera monitoring |
| Google Flood Forecasting / OpenHydroNet | Basin-level flood forecasting using hydrology, rainfall, streamflow, and catchment data | Local camera evidence review | Study later for forecasting ideas, not immediate MVP implementation |
| SAM 2 / YOLO segmentation | Helping mark water or river regions in images | Trusted flood warnings | Later for assisted labelling or water-region experiments |
| Classical computer vision | Cheap, explainable camera baselines like frame difference, optical flow, and reference-region change | Complex flood understanding by itself | Use now for the local MVP because it is simple, testable, and edge-friendly |
| FloodNet / satellite datasets | Learning flood-scene label ideas | Fixed river-camera monitoring | Research only for now |
| Vertex AI / Google Cloud Vision | Future cloud experiments and model management | Required edge operation or private-video workflow | Later only after privacy, cost, and data rules are clear |
| Rainfall / earthquake / external signals | Cross-checking whether a warning candidate makes sense | Main proof from the camera | Good future support signal, not the core MVP |

## Questions To Answer

At minimum, answer:

- Are we trying to detect flood/no flood, water rising/falling, water level, velocity, or a staged set of these?
- Do we train on full videos, frames, regions, or extracted measurements?
- Do we need to keep all videos/images, or only selected evidence and labels?
- How do we avoid training on private or unsafe data?
- Can OpenRiverCam outputs become optional upstream evidence records for OpenFloodAI?
- What should remain out of scope because it belongs to forecasting instead of camera evidence?
- What is the smallest useful camera-based ML experiment for this project?

## Safety Boundaries

This issue must not:

- train a production model
- upload private videos without a clear decision
- claim flood detection accuracy
- send alerts
- replace human review
- treat unverified labels as ground truth for production use
- make rainfall, earthquake, or forecast data the main MVP scope

## Expected Output

Create or update documentation with a short ML readiness plan.

Possible locations:

```text
docs/product/ml-readiness.md
docs/research/ml-model-options.md
```

or another existing docs location if the repository already has a better place.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A simple ML readiness plan exists in the docs.
- [ ] The plan explains that OpenFloodAI is camera-first for the current MVP.
- [ ] The plan explains what must be true before model training starts.
- [ ] The plan compares OpenRiverCam, Google Flood Forecasting, segmentation models, classical CV, datasets, cloud tools, and external signals.
- [ ] OpenRiverCam is treated as strong inspiration or possible integration for upstream camera monitoring.
- [ ] Google Flood Forecasting is treated as future forecasting research, not the immediate MVP path.
- [ ] Data privacy and safety boundaries are clear.
- [ ] The first possible camera-based ML experiment is described in plain language.
- [ ] No model training or production accuracy claim is added.

## Definition Of Done

The team can read the plan and know whether it is time to start ML work, what the first camera-based ML experiment should be, what role OpenRiverCam may play, and what must stay out of scope until later.

items.title: [FEATURE] Drag and drop video files to set active video
items.body:
**Which interface does this affect?**

- [x] GUI (desktop app)
- [ ] CLI (`trcc` commands)
- [ ] REST API (`trcc serve`)
- [ ] All / not sure

**Device (if relevant)**


**Is your feature request related to a problem?**

Opening files through menus is slow when testing or swapping videos frequently. Drag-and-drop provides a faster, more convenient workflow for quickly replacing or queuing videos during testing.

**Describe the solution you'd like**

Add OS drag-and-drop support so users can drop one or more video files onto the app window.

What should happen
- Drop a single supported video file onto the main window to replace the active video (optionally autoplay).
- Drop multiple supported files to append to the playlist in the order dropped.
- Show a semi-transparent drag overlay on the AIO preview area while dragging with short text like: "Drop to open video (Ctrl to queue)".
- Reject unsupported files and show a friendly toast, e.g.: "Could not load filename.ext — unsupported format or decode error."
- Support a modifier key for alternate behavior: plain drop = replace, Ctrl+drop = append.
- When replacing, preserve playback settings (looping, position) unless the user resets.

Acceptance criteria
- Files can be dropped from the OS file manager onto the main window and load without using the file picker.
- Common formats supported: mp4, mkv, avi, mov, webm, gif. Unsupported formats show an error toast.
- Drag overlay appears while dragging supported files and disappears on leave or drop.
- Single-file drops replace the active video by default; multi-file drops append to the playlist.
- Add a short README note or in-app tooltip describing the feature.

UI notes
- Overlay text: "Drop to open video (Ctrl to queue)".
- Success toast: "Loaded: filename.ext".
- Error toast: "Could not load filename.ext — unsupported format or decode error.".
- Show a loading indicator if decoding takes noticeable time.

Implementation notes
- Handle drag events using the GUI framework or OS APIs and reuse the existing video-loading pipeline so behavior matches the file picker.
- Add tests that simulate drop events where possible.
- Consider platform differences (Windows, macOS, Linux).

Additional context

Extra UX request: Add a "Video only" / "Clear overlays" control in Preview/Themes to temporarily hide overlays or persist as a saved theme.

items.title: [Feature]: Playlist — drop videos into a queue that auto-plays
items.body:
## What's the idea?

A queue in the panel: drop in YouTube videos, Netflix titles, or any castable URL, and Fling plays them in order — when one ends, the next starts, no trip back to the Mac.

## What problem does it solve?

Fling casts exactly one thing. A lecture series, a music-video run, or a kids' movie night means returning to the laptop after every item. A queue turns Fling into a set-and-forget session.

## Implementation notes

- **Adding items**: "Add tab to playlist" beside "Cast this tab" (reuses `TabProber`/`URLClassifier`), plus drag-and-drop of URLs onto the panel and "Add clipboard URL".
- **Advancing**: the cast pipeline already tracks progress for the panel's progress bar (`CastStatus` via catt polling). End-of-media detection triggers the next cast through the existing `CastPlanner` path.
- **Two item kinds, honestly handled**:
  - *Media items* (YouTube, direct files, sniffable streams) — true autoplay, cast via catt.
  - *App items* (a Netflix title) — Netflix won't stream through catt; the queue entry is an app deep link. Playing it launches the app on the title; end-of-playback detection is unreliable there, so app items are "up next, tap to play" rather than auto-advance. The UI should show which kind each entry is.
- **Persistence**: queue survives panel close; probably `AppState` + a small on-disk store.

## Done when

Queue three YouTube videos, walk away, come back to the third one playing. A Netflix title in the queue launches on tap and the panel says why it didn't auto-advance.

---

Part of #1

items.title: All three drop hotkeys emit the same task line, so a video clip arrives labelled 'dropped context'
items.body:
**What happened?**
The desktop app registers three distinct drop hotkeys (strings from /Applications/AG2 Space.app/Contents/MacOS/cinny):

    drop_context      control+shift+C
    drop_screenshot   control+S
    drop_video_clip   control+shift+R

All of them write the SAME task text into the engine:

    task: User dropped context via hotkey. Process this: <path>

(single occurrence in the binary, shared by every path).

Consequence, observed live on 2026-09-10: a control+shift+R screen recording arrived as
tasks/... with body 'User dropped context via hotkey. Process this: /var/folders/.../ag2-clip-1789078797258.mov'.
The file was a 9.34 GB, 2h48m35s QuickTime recording. Because the task says 'dropped context',
both the agent and the owner referred to it as a context drop for the entire exchange. The owner's
next message was literally 'Wait. Why I did context drop?' — he had pressed the video-clip hotkey,
not the context hotkey, and the task text gave neither of us any way to notice.

Why it matters beyond wording: context drop (control+shift+C) and video clip (control+shift+R) are
adjacent in the same modifier family, and they produce wildly different artifacts — a text selection
versus a multi-gigabyte screen recording. The task text is the only signal the agent gets about which
one fired, so a mis-press is undiagnosable from the agent side and the agent will confidently
describe a recording as a context drop.

Suggested fix: give each hotkey its own task line, e.g.
  drop_context      -> 'User dropped a text selection via hotkey (control+shift+C).'
  drop_screenshot   -> 'User dropped a screenshot via hotkey (control+S).'
  drop_video_clip   -> 'User dropped a screen recording via hotkey (control+shift+R).'
naming the artifact kind and the key that produced it.

items.title: Spec: Real Water pure-WebGPU Open Water runtime and Reference Experience
items.body:
## Problem Statement

Three.js developers do not have a reusable, production-grade open-ocean system that combines current WebGPU rendering, art-directable AAA presentation, gameplay-oriented water interaction, deterministic queries, exhaustive startup prewarming, and auditable quality gates. Existing examples usually demonstrate one narrow technique, rely on WebGL-era materials, compile work during visible gameplay, expose implementation details, or cannot integrate predictably into an existing Three.js host.

The user needs a pure-WebGPU route built on the latest tested Three.js revision, packaged as an open-source npm Module, with a controlled Reference Experience that proves the intended visual quality. The result must prioritize Perceptual Fidelity, visual composition, and gameplay over scientific solver purity; support Blender/glTF host models through explicit Interaction Shapes and Adapters; remain maintainable by AI agents; and distinguish claims made for the controlled Reference Experience from behavior available to arbitrary Host Integrations.

## Solution

Create Real Water as an MIT-licensed, TypeScript, ESM-only npm Module for native Three.js. It will run only on a verified Core WebGPU backend, use TSL and public NodeMaterial/RenderPipeline facilities by default, and reject WebGL fallback and WebGPU Compatibility Mode.

Real Water will own one active Open Water Domain per renderer. A multi-cascade spectral ocean will supply large-scale motion, a movable local interaction field will supply wakes and impacts around an Interaction Anchor, and a layered optical and secondary-effects pipeline will provide reflections, refraction, scattering, whitewater, Hero Breakers, spray, waterline, underwater volume, caustics, bubbles, weather, and temporal stability. The runtime will expose deep Startup and command/query Interfaces rather than internal render nodes or solvers.

Before any 3D frame becomes visible, an independent Loading Experience will execute a fail-closed Readiness Gate over a versioned Prewarm Manifest. It will initialize resources, compile reachable render variants, execute compute kernels against scratch state, run hidden RenderPipeline routes, prime temporal histories, verify GPU completion, and render a main-camera guard frame. Undeclared structural variants will never compile visibly at first use.

The published runtime will accept host-owned renderer, scene, camera, time, rigid bodies, and assets through narrow Host, Body Physics, and Environment Adapter seams. Callers will update Artistic Controls and the Interaction Anchor, submit batched Disturbances, attach bodies using closed Interaction Shapes, run allocation-free batched Gameplay Queries, and inspect lightweight state. Structural changes will require a new preparation run.

A controlled Reference Experience will provide Director, Sandbox, and QA modes; accessible Artist and Engineering control presenters; versioned Water, Environment, Quality, and Showcase presets; deterministic capture routes; and three authored looks. It alone will receive the Native Quality and whole-frame performance claim. Demonstration objects will be generated as consistent image Reference Packs and then reconstructed as independently verified code-only procedural Three.js models.

## User Stories

1. As a Three.js developer, I want to install Real Water from npm, so that I can add an advanced ocean without copying a demo into my application.
2. As a Three.js developer, I want Real Water to use Three.js as a peer dependency, so that my application and the plugin share one compatible runtime.
3. As a Three.js developer, I want an ESM-only package with declarations and source maps, so that modern browser tooling can tree-shake and debug it cleanly.
4. As a host developer, I want Real Water to accept my renderer, scene, and camera, so that it can integrate without creating a second hidden application.
5. As a host developer, I want Real Water to preserve ownership of my renderer, scene, camera, assets, and rigid bodies, so that disposal cannot destroy host state.
6. As a host developer, I want a clear compatibility report before startup completes, so that unsupported devices fail with actionable reasons.
7. As a host developer, I want WebGL fallback rejected explicitly, so that a compute-dependent ocean never silently runs on the wrong backend.
8. As a host developer, I want Compatibility Mode rejected for the promised quality path, so that missing Core WebGPU limits do not produce an ambiguous degraded experience.
9. As a host developer, I want a versioned Prewarm Manifest, so that every structural effect and resource required by my integration is declared before use.
10. As an end user, I want to see a responsive Loading Experience immediately, so that compilation never looks like a frozen or blank page.
11. As an end user, I want the first visible 3D frame to be complete and stable, so that I never see shader compilation, black materials, stale history, or a wrong camera.
12. As an end user, I want a readable startup error with retry and diagnostics, so that failure does not reveal a broken partial scene.
13. As a host developer, I want startup progress to represent completed manifest work, so that the loading UI never invents a misleading percentage or ETA.
14. As a host developer, I want to cancel preparation safely, so that navigation or teardown does not leak resources.
15. As a host developer, I want preparation and disposal to be idempotent at their documented seams, so that lifecycle recovery is predictable.
16. As a host developer, I want an undeclared effect to fail with a structural error, so that no shader compiles during visible runtime.
17. As a host developer, I want device loss to invalidate the runtime explicitly, so that I can recreate the renderer and prepare again.
18. As a Reference Experience viewer, I want device loss to return me to the Loading Experience for one rebuild attempt, so that recovery is graceful but bounded.
19. As a Reference Experience viewer, I want an open ocean extending to the horizon, so that the scene reads as ocean-scale rather than a tiled pool.
20. As an artist, I want calm, swell, and storm sea characters, so that one runtime can support distinct moods.
21. As an artist, I want independent control of swell drama, directionality, choppiness, crest sharpness, micro detail, and time scale, so that the ocean can be directed visually.
22. As an artist, I want distant wave detail to remain stable and non-repetitive, so that the horizon does not expose obvious tiling or shimmer.
23. As a viewer, I want near waves to use geometry, middle-distance waves to use normal detail, and subpixel waves to use filtered slope statistics, so that detail transitions are continuous.
24. As a viewer, I want convincing Fresnel, sun glitter, reflection, refraction, absorption, scattering, and crest transmission, so that the surface looks like water in varied lighting.
25. As a viewer, I want local reflections to fall back smoothly to planar or environment reflection, so that SSR misses never become black holes.
26. As a viewer, I want whitecaps to form, move, break up, and decay over time, so that foam behaves as a persistent effect rather than flickering noise.
27. As an artist, I want whitecap amount, foam persistence, breakup, detail, brightness, and subsurface response controls, so that whitewater supports composition.
28. As a viewer, I want spray, droplets, mist, and storm aerosol, so that energetic water has readable scale and violence.
29. As a viewer, I want art-directed Hero Breakers in focal locations, so that dramatic breaking silhouettes are possible without a full volumetric fluid solver.
30. As a viewer, I want rain ripples, rain spray, cloud-shadow response, and lightning response, so that the ocean belongs to the weather system.
31. As a viewer, I want a stable waterline transition, so that crossing the surface does not pop, smear, or reveal stale buffers.
32. As an underwater viewer, I want absorption, fog, volumetric scattering, shadows, sun shafts, and depth-dependent color, so that underwater space has scale and atmosphere.
33. As an underwater viewer, I want bounded dynamic caustics on visible receivers, so that surface motion affects underwater lighting.
34. As an underwater viewer, I want suspended particles, bubble clouds, rising bubbles, and water-film transitions, so that the environment feels inhabited and wet.
35. As a gameplay developer, I want a synchronous batched Gameplay Query Interface, so that gameplay can sample height, normal, velocity, and foam without waiting for GPU readback.
36. As a gameplay developer, I want every Gameplay Query result tagged with tick, control revision, and local snapshot age, so that I can reason about coherence and latency.
37. As a gameplay developer, I want base spectral queries to use the same seed as rendering, so that floating objects follow the visible ocean.
38. As a gameplay developer, I want local interaction corrections to be at most one tick old, so that wakes and impacts remain responsive without a synchronous GPU stall.
39. As a physics integrator, I want to attach a rigid body through a Body Physics Adapter, so that Real Water does not depend on one physics engine.
40. As a physics integrator, I want to provide a closed Interaction Shape separate from the render mesh, so that hydrodynamic work remains bounded and predictable.
41. As a physics integrator, I want support for spheres, boxes, capsules, convex hulls, and compounds, so that common vessel and prop proxies can be represented.
42. As a physics integrator, I want water loads applied before my fixed physics integration, so that buoyancy and drag affect the intended tick.
43. As a gameplay developer, I want 60 Hz water and body coupling with 30 FPS presentation interpolation, so that visual frame rate does not reduce control responsiveness.
44. As a gameplay developer, I want buoyancy, drag, slamming, stabilizing torque, and wakes, so that boats and props respond believably.
45. As a gameplay developer, I want to move one Interaction Anchor, so that high-detail interaction follows the hero object rather than simulating the entire world.
46. As a gameplay developer, I want to submit radial impacts, directional wakes, foam bursts, and Hero Breakers in batches, so that transient events cross the Interface efficiently.
47. As a gameplay developer, I want propeller and bow/stern effects generated from body sockets, so that I do not submit the same Disturbance manually every tick.
48. As a gameplay developer, I want predictable capacity and overflow receipts, so that overload never triggers a hidden allocation or missing effect without explanation.
49. As an artist, I want hot Artistic Controls to change smoothly, so that I can tune the ocean without returning to the loading screen.
50. As an engineer, I want structural controls separated from Artistic Controls, so that resource and pipeline changes cannot masquerade as live tuning.
51. As an engineer, I want Quality Profile edits to require Apply and Reload, so that structural changes pass the Readiness Gate.
52. As an artist, I want a curated Artist presenter with semantic labels and accessible controls, so that I can tune water without reading solver variables.
53. As an engineer, I want an Engineering presenter with throttled monitors and debug controls, so that I can inspect timing and state without polluting the artist workflow.
54. As an artist, I want Artist and Engineering presenters to consume one control schema, so that UI ranges and runtime behavior cannot drift.
55. As an artist, I want versioned Water Presets, so that authored sea looks survive UI-library upgrades.
56. As a scene author, I want Environment Presets separate from Water Presets, so that changing weather does not mutate ocean structure.
57. As a performance engineer, I want Quality Profiles separate from visual presets, so that resource sizes and pass layouts remain explicit.
58. As a presentation author, I want Showcase Presets combining water, environment, quality, camera, and events, so that demonstrations are deterministic and replayable.
59. As a Reference Experience viewer, I want Calm Sunrise, Blue Noon Swell, and Storm Front looks, so that the system demonstrates a meaningful visual range.
60. As a Reference Experience viewer, I want a directed showcase loop, so that the strongest effects are presented without setup.
61. As a Reference Experience user, I want a Sandbox mode, so that I can drive the vessel, move the camera, pause, reset, and tune parameters.
62. As a QA engineer, I want a test-only QA mode, so that fixed ticks, cameras, events, and named buffers are directly controllable.
63. As a preset author, I want local import, export, copy, rename, restore, and migration, so that my settings remain portable and recoverable.
64. As a preset author, I want invalid or future preset JSON preserved, so that incompatible data is never silently destroyed.
65. As a privacy-conscious user, I want the core runtime to perform no analytics, persistence, cookies, or hidden network calls, so that integration remains local and predictable.
66. As a host developer, I want Environment input supplied explicitly, so that Real Water never guesses my sun, sky, wind, or weather.
67. As a host developer, I want Reference, manual Three, and memory Host Adapters, so that production and deterministic tests exercise the same lifecycle seam.
68. As a maintainer, I want heavy diagnostics separate from the common Runtime Interface, so that normal execution has no accidental GPU readback or profiler overhead.
69. As a maintainer, I want a lightweight inspect operation, so that common state can be observed without enabling detailed diagnostics.
70. As a QA engineer, I want final color and named water buffers captured at exact ticks, so that failures can be localized beyond a full-screen screenshot.
71. As a QA engineer, I want region-specific gates for the horizon, waterline, glints, wake, foam, SSR, and underwater effects, so that a global score cannot hide a critical local defect.
72. As a QA engineer, I want deterministic motion-vector and history tests, so that temporal ghosting and shimmer are caught before release.
73. As a QA engineer, I want Chrome traces, displayed-frame intervals, dropped-frame classifications, and GPU attribution kept as separate evidence, so that one profiler cannot distort or replace another.
74. As a performance engineer, I want Native Quality tested at an exact 2560 by 1440 drawing buffer with no temporal upscaling, so that the performance claim is unambiguous.
75. As a performance engineer, I want five deterministic ten-minute runs on the reference M5 Mac, so that thermal and background instability cannot be hidden by one favorable run.
76. As a performance engineer, I want average FPS, tail-mean one-percent-low, percentile frame times, hitch ratio, dropped frames, cadence misses, CPU time, and GPU time gated independently, so that stable presentation is proven rather than inferred from average FPS.
77. As a performance engineer, I want profiler-on and profiler-off control runs, so that instrumentation overhead cannot validate itself.
78. As a release maintainer, I want Chrome certification and Safari regression results kept separate, so that samples from different browser pipelines are not mixed.
79. As a CI maintainer, I want GitHub Actions treated as a regression detector rather than Native certification authority, so that software or non-reference GPU results never become a false quality claim.
80. As a maintainer, I want explicit Three.js revision compatibility, so that experimental WebGPU API changes trigger deliberate migration and regression work.
81. As a maintainer, I want TSL-first shader code, so that public Three integration, typing, and AI-assisted maintenance stay local and reviewable.
82. As a maintainer, I want raw WGSL isolated behind an internal seam and justified by profiling, so that low-level optimization does not spread version coupling.
83. As a maintainer, I want API Extractor reports committed for every published package, so that public Interface changes are intentional.
84. As an npm consumer, I want package exports to prevent unsupported deep imports, so that internal refactors do not become accidental breaking changes.
85. As an npm consumer, I want the package to remain below version 1.0 until its Interfaces survive real integrations, so that early changes are communicated honestly.
86. As an npm consumer, I want comprehensive native Three integration documentation, so that startup, runtime, adapters, queries, presets, errors, and responsibility boundaries are understandable.
87. As a maintainer, I want exact-pinned development tools and a frozen workspace lockfile, so that AI-generated changes build deterministically.
88. As a maintainer, I want core packages compiled by TypeScript without overlapping bundlers, so that build ownership and debugging remain simple.
89. As a maintainer, I want fast in-process tests separated from real-browser tests, so that each test runner has one clear purpose.
90. As an accessibility user, I want loading and Artist controls to support keyboard, screen-reader text, focus, contrast, and reduced motion, so that the Reference Experience is operable without relying on a dense engineering panel.
91. As an asset maintainer, I want a shared Reference Bible, so that generated demonstration objects belong to one visual world.
92. As an asset maintainer, I want one approved identity anchor before derivative views, so that image generation does not drift between angles.
93. As an asset maintainer, I want neutral modeling references separated from cinematic concept art, so that procedural reconstruction is not confused by fog, splash, or strong perspective.
94. As an asset maintainer, I want every approved Reference Pack to retain its final prompt, provenance, versions, and known inconsistencies, so that the process remains auditable.
95. As an asset maintainer, I want imagegen references converted into independent code-only procedural models through img2threejs gates, so that runtime assets remain maintainable Three.js code rather than opaque generated meshes.
96. As a gameplay developer, I want the hero vessel model to expose bow, stern, propeller, wake, and interaction anchors, so that visual geometry and water behavior connect correctly.
97. As a reviewer, I want every procedural model pass to include comparisons and honest remaining differences, so that passing a score never overstates fidelity.
98. As a license reviewer, I want generated assets, dependencies, and future external materials recorded in a license inventory, so that the MIT package can be distributed safely.
99. As a release maintainer, I want alpha previews before public 0.1.0, so that integration feedback can improve Interfaces without weakening final gates.
100. As a project owner, I want public 0.1.0 blocked until every accepted gate passes, so that the initial release reflects the agreed quality bar.
101. As a Reference Experience viewer, I want the generated subjects composed into the scene I am shown, so that the demonstration reads as an inhabited sea rather than empty water around a proxy.
102. As a reviewer, I want each Demonstration Subject to declare which Reference Experience modes it participates in, and to be checked as reachable in the built application, so that a model that ships nothing cannot be mistaken for a verified one.

## Implementation Decisions

- Aesthetic Authority is the highest product rule: physical models are used only when they improve Perceptual Fidelity, coherence, or gameplay.
- The first release supports Open Water only: ocean and great-lake scale, one Open Water Domain per WebGPURenderer, one sea level, and one Interaction Anchor.
- The coordinate contract is Three.js Y-up, horizontal XZ water, one unit per metre, with host floating-origin shifts. Tilted water planes, multiple simultaneous oceans, rivers, and pools are not represented by this runtime.
- The tested Three.js baseline is 0.185.1. The published peer range is at least 0.185.1 and below 0.186.0; the development dependency is exact.
- The runtime verifies a real Core WebGPU backend after asynchronous renderer initialization. WebGL fallback and WebGPU Compatibility Mode fail closed.
- Materials, compute, and render composition use public TSL and NodeMaterial facilities by default. Raw WGSL is an internal, measured escape hatch and may not depend on public callers knowing Three backend details.
- Three revision-sensitive behavior is concentrated in one internal Adapter. Current r185 limitations require conditional variant staging, scratch compute execution, hidden RenderPipeline rendering, GPU completion probing, and a main-camera guard frame.
- The public startup Module exposes preparation as a cancellable run and returns a usable lease only after the Readiness Gate. Progress is based on completed manifest work; errors are structured; disposal is idempotent and preserves host-owned resources.
- The Reference Experience wraps startup with an independent Loading Experience that is visible before WebGPU work begins and remains opaque until the first stable 3D frame is ready.
- Every effect route, material and MRT variant, render target, compute kernel, asset, and conditional state used by a prepared runtime is declared by a versioned Prewarm Manifest.
- Each page load repeats the Readiness Gate. Browser shader caches or stored hashes may not bypass it.
- Compute kernels are warmed by executing against scratch resources and restoring deterministic state. RenderPipeline and temporal routes are warmed by hidden rendering.
- Every conditional route primes eight hidden history frames, then performs a completion readback and main-camera guard frame before visibility.
- Runtime structural extension is absent in the first release. A structural change disposes the current lease and performs a complete new preparation.
- An undeclared runtime effect or variant returns EFFECT_NOT_PREWARMED and never compiles visibly.
- The ready runtime uses an Adapter-driven command/query Interface. Callers do not coordinate internal render or physics steps directly.
- The common Runtime Interface exposes read-only capabilities, hot Artistic Controls, Interaction Anchor updates, batched Gameplay Queries, batched Disturbances, body attachment, lightweight inspection, and lease disposal.
- Reference, manual Three, and memory Host Adapters are provided. Host Adapter ordering keeps fixed water/body steps separate from presentation and owns the valid RenderPipeline integration.
- Body Physics and Environment are public Adapter seams. Core imports no physics engine, framework, UI library, persistence library, or host application.
- The host owns monotonic simulation time. The runtime never reads wall-clock time for authoritative state.
- Reference Gameplay Coupling runs at fixed 60 Hz and presentation at evenly paced 30 FPS with interpolation. Long gaps are bounded rather than producing an unbounded catch-up spiral.
- Base spectral Gameplay Queries use the same deterministic seed as rendering on the CPU. Local GPU interaction correction uses the latest completed snapshot and reports zero-or-one-tick age.
- Gameplay Queries are batched and use caller-owned typed arrays. Outputs contain height, normal, three-dimensional surface velocity, foam, simulation tick, Artistic Control revision, and local snapshot age.
- The first structural capacity target is 32 attached bodies, 128 active Disturbances, 2,048 query points per fixed tick, eight Hero Breakers, and 131,072 secondary particles, subject to final measured freezing.
- Supported Interaction Shapes are spheres, boxes, capsules, closed convex hulls of at most 64 vertices, and compounds of at most 32 children. Render triangles are never implicit water boundaries.
- Body and query overflow is a structured error. Disturbance overflow drops the lowest visual priority with a receipt. Particle pressure reduces low-contribution density without eliminating the effect or allocating new structural buffers.
- Public manual Disturbances are radial impacts, directional wakes, foam bursts, and Hero Breakers. Body sockets generate propeller and bow/stern effects.
- Interaction Shapes are immutable for a Body lease. Bodies may attach and detach within prepared capacity.
- Environment scalars can update each fixed tick. Replacing an environment texture identity, format, or size is structural and requires re-preparation.
- Artistic Controls use perceptual language and may update smoothly. Cascade count, grids, formats, capacities, pass layout, effect set, AA route, and resource identities belong to an immutable Quality Profile.
- Water, Environment, Quality, and Showcase presets are separate versioned schemas. Engineering edits structural drafts and applies them only through the Loading Experience.
- Native Quality is the highest real-time Reference Experience contract: exact 2560 by 1440 drawing buffer, render scale 1.0, native-resolution TRAA, SDR sRGB output, every in-scope subsystem enabled or deterministically triggered, and no TAAU, dynamic resolution, frame generation, or MSAA.
- Auxiliary pass sizes may be lower than output resolution only after final-image and temporal quality gates. Cinematic Maximum may raise them without a real-time performance claim.
- Native uses custom procedural motion vectors, history rejection, explicit history resets, and post-TRAA output-resolution composition for transparent spray, mist, and lens droplets.
- Reflection combines environment, planar, and SSR layers with explicit miss fallback. Refraction is depth-aware. Optical controls cover microfacet response, Fresnel, sun glints, absorption, scattering, crest transmission, foam overrides, and subpixel filtering.
- The Open Water simulation combines four art-directed spectral bands with non-periodic blending and near-geometry, middle-normal, and far-slope transitions.
- A camera-relative clipmap or projected grid presents the surface. The local interaction field follows the Interaction Anchor and fades into the spectral surface.
- Whitewater is layered persistent foam, subsurface foam/bubbles, secondary particles, mist, and sparse art-directed Hero Breakers. A general real-time multiphase solver is deliberately excluded.
- Underwater rendering includes stable waterline state, underside Fresnel and total internal reflection, absorption, fog, volumetric scattering and shadows, sun shafts, bounded caustics, depth color, particles, bubbles, wetness transition, and exposure/color grading.
- Weather integration includes wind, gusts, rain ripples and spray, cloud shadows, lightning, horizon haze, atmospheric composition, and distant-island integration.
- The complete confirmed Native effect manifest and performance formulas are maintained as durable research evidence and become versioned QA inputs.
- Only the controlled Reference Experience receives final visual and whole-frame performance guarantees. Host Integrations receive contracts, capability checks, diagnostics, controls, and module-level behavior but own their final image and frame rate.
- The Reference Experience provides Director, Sandbox, and QA modes and Calm Sunrise, Blue Noon Swell, and Storm Front authored presets.
- Artist mode is an accessible custom semantic DOM presenter. Engineering mode lazy-loads an exactly pinned Tweakpane Adapter. Both consume one control schema; Tweakpane state is not a durable preset format.
- The test-only QA Harness controls reset, explicit fixed ticks, cameras, event schedules, presentation, named-buffer capture, and inspection. It is not exposed in production builds.
- The Reference Experience stores presets locally with explicit versioning and migrations. Core performs no network, storage, cookie, or analytics operation.
- Demonstration assets use a consistent offshore research/rescue Reference Bible. Built-in image generation produces approved raster Reference Packs; img2threejs produces independent code-only procedural models under staged visual and structural gates.
- The initial generated subjects are a roughly 14 m hero research/rescue vessel, navigation buoy, marine crate, underwater structure, and basalt sea stack. Brands and generated text are excluded.
- Each generated subject is a Demonstration Subject that declares its Scene Participation: the Reference Experience modes it is composed into and the water behavior it carries in each. Director, Sandbox, and QA compose from one shared scene assembly, and a committed check asserts every declared Subject is reachable from the production entry point of the built application rather than merely present in the repository.
- The package name target is real-water under MIT. Adapter packages remain separate. Name availability is rechecked before publication.
- The workspace uses exact-pinned Node 24 and pnpm 11, TypeScript project references, tsc-built unbundled ESM packages, Vite for the private app, Vitest for fast tests, Playwright for browser tests, API Extractor for public Interface reports, ESLint flat config, and separate Prettier checks.
- Releases remain 0.x until startup, runtime, query, and Adapter Interfaces survive real integrations. Public 0.1.0 is blocked by every accepted visual, startup, performance, API, documentation, compatibility, and license gate.

## Testing Decisions

- Tests assert observable behavior through the highest available seam and do not inspect internal TSL graphs, render targets, pipeline caches, solver classes, or private scheduling state.
- The Startup Interface is the primary seam for manifest validation, progress, cancellation, retry policy, failure classification, readiness, ownership, and disposal.
- The ready Runtime command/query Interface is the primary seam for controls, body attachment, Environment and Host Adapters, Disturbances, Gameplay Queries, capacities, lifecycle, suspension, invalidation, and disposal.
- Memory Host, Body Physics, Environment, Loading Presenter, clock, and prewarm Adapters provide deterministic test implementations at the same seams used by production.
- Browser rendering is tested through the explicit QA Harness rather than time-based sleeps or arbitrary requestAnimationFrame polling.
- Deterministic manifests pin Three, browser, OS profile, seeds, drawing buffer, auxiliary targets, Quality Profile, presets, fixed ticks, camera paths, body paths, weather, event schedules, and capture points.
- Named captures include final color, water-only color, silhouette/alpha, linear depth, normal, motion vectors, foam/history, SSR hit/confidence, and effect identity where useful.
- Visual gates are layered: hard geometry/waterline checks, same-platform pixel comparisons, linear color error, region-specific thresholds, temporal change metrics, and human comparison sheets.
- A global image score may not override failure of a critical region such as the waterline, horizon, hero wake, foam, reflection fallback, or underwater visibility.
- Temporal tests cover fast camera motion, glints, thin foam, high-speed vessel motion, waterline crossing, camera cuts, origin shifts, effect transitions, disocclusion, history rejection, and transparent post-TRAA effects.
- Vitest covers pure schemas, public Interface behavior, deterministic state, capacity rules, preset migrations, query packing, Adapter ordering, and error contracts.
- Playwright covers Loading Experience behavior, Core WebGPU rejection, real WebGPURenderer and RenderPipeline integration, QA Harness control, screenshots, console/device errors, and environment-specific smoke tests.
- Playwright screenshot baselines are generated and compared only on matching OS, browser, hardware, power, and headless/headed profiles.
- Playwright video and action trace are failure diagnostics, not Native visual or cadence evidence.
- GitHub Actions performs frozen install, lint, format, type, build, unit, manifest, API report, packed-package, loading, capability-rejection, and profile-labeled WebGPU smoke tests.
- Standard CI runners never sign the Native Quality claim. Software WebGPU, Linux GPU, and non-reference Mac baselines remain separate.
- The reference M5 Mac in headed Chrome is the acceptance authority for Native screenshots, temporal review, Chrome performance trace, GPU attribution, and whole-frame performance.
- Native certification runs at fixed 60 Hz display mode, exact 2560 by 1440, full Native manifest, panel state frozen, AC power, Low Power Mode off, and no visible profiler or DevTools UI.
- The certification route warms for 60 seconds, runs deterministically for ten minutes, and repeats five times; all five runs must pass.
- Confirmed Native performance gates are average displayed FPS at least 30; tail-mean one-percent-low at least 30; p99 displayed interval at most 34 ms; p99.9 at most 50 ms; p99 CPU and GPU production time each at most 28 ms; hitch ratio below 5 ms per second; dropped or partially presented active frames at most 0.1 percent; no consecutive drops; no post-prewarm interval above 100 ms; at most one cadence miss in the worst rolling second; and at most 3 percent relative one-percent-low spread across runs.
- An uncapped run measures headroom, a normal ProMotion run evaluates experience, and Safari 27 runs separately. These samples are never merged with fixed-60-Hz Chrome certification.
- Detailed GPU diagnostics are disabled by default. Profiler-on and profiler-off runs measure observer overhead and memory behavior.
- Every resource, format, variant, conditional effect, and debug route used by a test must be represented in the Prewarm Manifest before visibility.
- Cold startup and first activation of every conditional route are tested separately from steady-state certification. The loading-time ceiling is frozen only after an end-to-end prototype supplies evidence.
- API Extractor reports and packed-package tests gate the public npm surface. Published tests resolve built exports rather than source aliases.
- img2threejs model testing uses its required state, intake, strict spec, pass, screenshot, multi-angle, attachment, action-ready, and part-coverage gates. A passing image score does not prove a complete or correct model.
- The repository currently has no implementation tests; the above Startup, Runtime, QA Harness, and Reference Experience seams are the agreed prior art for the first code.

## Out of Scope

- Rivers, canals, waterfalls, floods, pools, arbitrary water topology, and multiple simultaneous water domains.
- Near-shore shoaling, surf generation, wet/dry boundaries, beach wetness, terrain erosion, and physically simulated coastline hydrodynamics.
- Full three-dimensional Navier-Stokes, general air-water multiphase simulation, particle-resolved breakup, and scientifically conservative fluid-structure interaction.
- Scientifically accurate ocean forecasting, measured physical parameter fidelity, server-authoritative ocean state, lockstep networking, and multiplayer determinism.
- Arbitrary render triangle meshes as exact fluid boundaries.
- Runtime structural pipeline creation, incremental startup mutation, invisible compilation, or undeclared effect activation.
- WebGL fallback, WebGPU Compatibility Mode parity, mobile quality parity, or the same visual claim on unsupported hardware.
- Final-image and whole-frame performance guarantees for arbitrary Host Integrations.
- Multiple player cameras, split-screen, XR, controller, touch, and mobile Reference Experience input in the first release.
- Audio assets, water audio simulation, and a bundled audio engine. Semantic events may support a future host Audio Adapter.
- Cinematic Maximum real-time performance guarantees.
- Decorative chromatic water dispersion, default motion blur, default depth of field, or strong sharpening used to hide temporal defects.
- Bundling Three.js, shipping CJS, exposing internal TSL nodes/materials/render targets/compute kernels, or supporting untested Three revisions.
- React Three Fiber and Rapier as core dependencies. They may become separate future Adapter packages.
- Automatic cloud sync, analytics, remote preset storage, hidden CDN asset fetching, or core localStorage use.
- Third-party art packs, branded assets, unverifiable textures, or generated text/markings in demonstration references.
- Immediate GitHub self-hosted execution on the personal M5 machine.

## Further Notes

- The repository currently contains the domain glossary, ADR-0001 through ADR-0025, the Native Quality research/effect manifest, and a GitHub implementation map with nine dependent milestone issues. No implementation code has been created.
- Existing GitHub map issue #1 remains the coordination surface; this issue is the complete product and engineering specification.
- The nine milestone issues cover foundations; spectral Open Water; surface optics and temporal rendering; local interaction and runtime contracts; whitewater and weather; underwater; Reference Experience; generated/procedural assets; and final optimization/certification/release.
- Exact auxiliary pass sizes, final capacity ceilings, and loading-time thresholds remain evidence-derived implementation outcomes. Changing them may not weaken the accepted visual or performance gates.
- Three.js WebGPU APIs are experimental. Each revision change requires a concentrated internal Adapter update, public Interface review, complete prewarm regression, and recertification where behavior or output changes.
- The user has confirmed that this specification reflects the complete shared understanding reached through the design interview.

items.title: [bug]: input_video chat content part payload is dropped
items.body:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I have searched existing issues and discussions to avoid duplicates

### Description

`input_video` chat content parts lose their payload passing through Bifrost. The `type` survives, the body does not, so the backend receives a video part with no data and rejects the request.

This is the shape used by llama.cpp-based backends (`input_video.data` as raw base64, or `input_video.url`), mirroring `input_audio`. #5500 covers the `video_url` shape used by vLLM/Qwen — this is the other shape and is not addressed by it.

`image_url` and `input_audio` pass through fine.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure an OpenAI-compatible provider backed by a server that accepts `input_video`, with a video-capable model.
2. Send a chat completion containing:

```json
{"role": "user", "content": [
  {"type": "input_video", "input_video": {"data": "<raw base64>"}},
  {"type": "text", "text": "describe this video"}
]}
```

3. Send the identical request straight to the backend for comparison.

### Expected behavior

The gateway returns the model's answer, as the direct request does.

### Actual behavior

The gateway returns 500 relaying a backend decode failure, with `is_bifrost_error: false`. The direct request succeeds.

### Affected area(s)

Core (Go)

### Version

v1.6.11

### Severity

Medium

items.body:
## Report
Dragging image, audio, or video files into the TUI composer does not always reliably produce an attachment/path mask. This affects both individual files and multi-file drops. User-reported; root cause and terminal-specific reproduction remain to be investigated.

## Expected behavior / acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dropping a supported image, audio, or video file reliably creates its composer attachment mask.
- [ ] Dropping multiple files reliably recognizes and masks each supported attachment, preserving order and association with the original path.
- [ ] Cover paths containing spaces and shell quoting/escaping as emitted by terminal drag-and-drop, and consecutive drops.
- [ ] Masks remain associated with the correct payload through editing and submission; no silently omitted or duplicated attachments.
- [ ] Unsupported media or failed recognition follows existing validation behavior without silently losing input.
- [ ] Add regression tests for single/multiple image, audio, and video paths and document the terminal/platform reproduction used for verification.

## Related
#330 owns a composer/attachment/paste refactor, but explicitly excludes behavior changes; this issue tracks the user-visible reliability fix.
